edges.effect_quant: The pooled childhood-cancer literature consistently suggests a modest reduction in leukemia risk among children who were breastfed, with relative-risk estimates usually clustering around 10% to 25% lower risk.
edges.population: children with any or longer-duration breastfeeding exposure
edges.mechanism: Breast milk shapes infant immune development, microbial colonization, and inflammatory signaling during the exact window when early immune programming may matter for leukemia susceptibility. That makes the signal biologically plausible even if the effect size is modest.
edges.summary: The strongest anchor here is the large dose-response childhood-cancer meta-analysis, which found lower leukemia risk among breastfed children. Newer umbrella work and a focused early-life leukemia review did not overturn that finding; they mainly narrowed it into a modest but fairly repeatable protective association.
edges.caveats: This is still observational literature, so residual confounding by socioeconomic patterning, parental behaviors, and correlated early-life exposures is hard to remove completely. The safest read is modest protection, not a dramatic shield effect.

evidence.notes: Early Life Nutrition Factors and Risk of Acute Leukemia in Children: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

evidence.citation: Fan D et al 2023 J Glob Health
evidence.notes: Role of breastfeeding on maternal and childhood cancers: An umbrella review of meta-analyses.

effect_quant.comparator: ever breastfeeding versus never breastfeeding for childhood leukemia
